entities.summary: The worthwhile version of famous Kitayamazaki is a strenuous trail through forest, fishing settlements, stairs and 200 m-class sea cliffs rather than a drive-up lookout.
entities.description: Northern Sanriku's coast repeatedly hides and reveals the sea as the Michinoku Coastal Trail climbs and descends through cliff-top forest, coves and settlements. Around Tsukuehama, historic fishing access adds hand-cut passages and local landscape history. Official stages around Tanohata–Kitayamazaki and north toward Fudai are physically harder than their kilometre counts suggest because of accumulated ascent and stairs.
entities.whyWorthwhile: Walking converts a famous static panorama into one of the strongest under-recognized mainland sea-cliff journeys found in the research. The sustained physical relationship with the coast is the reason to allocate a full day or two.

entities.summary: An island-scale wall of stratified, tilted and folded sea cliffs combines with barrier lakes, villages and road viewpoints; a small-boat cruise adds the strongest sense of scale.
entities.description: The Koshiki Islands are valuable as a geological system rather than one formation. Long western cliff walls expose sedimentary layers at monumental scale while the opposite side adds lagoons, sand bars, settlements and bridge engineering. Land travel is substantial enough to justify the trip on its own, but calm-sea cliff cruises reveal structures and vertical scale that are hard to read from shore.
entities.whyWorthwhile: This was one of the research run's credible E5 landscapes: a coherent island-scale geological coast whose science transfers directly into spectacle, while still retaining worthwhile terrestrial scenery when boats cannot sail.

entities.summary: Kilometres of smooth welded-tuff riverbed, potholes, shallow clear water and old beech forest turn the gorge floor itself into the walking experience.
entities.description: In Oku-Moriyoshi, water has polished broad welded-tuff channels into a continuous walking environment rather than a sequence of isolated waterfalls. The maintained Todo route is the conservative version: roughly an 8 km return outing with little elevation. Akamizu is more immersive and repeatedly enters the stream; the full Todo–Akamizu connection can cross into technical canyon terrain and should not be inferred to be ordinary hiking.
entities.whyWorthwhile: The unusual value is sustained contact with the stone-and-water floor of the gorge. In early to mid-October the polished rock, clear water and beech autumn colour create one of the research run's strongest destination-worthy landscapes.

entities.summary: A compact whole-island journey links nearly treeless pasture, cattle and horses, old stone walls, villages and oxidized red volcanic sea cliffs.
entities.description: Chiburijima, the smallest inhabited Dōzen island, works because its landscapes remain coherent while moving through them. Akahage-yama opens into broad grazed uplands, old stone walls and ocean views before roads descend toward the vividly oxidized Akakabe cliff and small settlements. A roughly 27 km circuit is practical by reserved scooter or car; cycling is possible but exposed and hilly.
entities.whyWorthwhile: Unlike an island built around a single viewpoint, Chiburijima combines pasture history, volcanic geology and settlement in one continuous small-scale journey. It is a strong reason not to stop Oki research at Nishinoshima.

entities.summary: A full recreated Edo-period town built around role-play, ninja and samurai activities, interactive houses and live entertainment rather than passive historical display.
entities.description: Children can train as ninja or samurai and solve period-themed missions; adults can join selected samurai experiences, while maze houses, ninja mechanisms, archery and throwing-star activities make the town itself playable. Japanese improves narrative shows, but much of the environment and activity remains visually legible.
entities.whyWorthwhile: One of Japan’s most convincing historical theme-park experiences and worth substantial regional travel. Some activities cost extra and spoken-Japanese shows lose nuance without the language, but the destination remains strong beyond those components.

entities.summary: A still-inhabited former company town pairs a guided underground mine trolley experience with unusually direct surface access to Japan's postwar coal-mining landscape.
entities.description: Ikeshima is not simply another abandoned mining island. Visitors can enter preserved underground workings on a fixed guided experience, historically led by former miners, then walk through a contracting but still inhabited company settlement containing housing and industrial remains. This combination of machinery, oral testimony, underground space and everyday island fabric made it the research run's most urgent industrial discovery.
entities.whyWorthwhile: Hashima dominates the mining-island narrative, but Ikeshima offers more direct engagement with lived mining history. The underground experience is scheduled to end at the close of March 2027, making current planning time-critical.

entities.summary: A broad Miocene wave-cut platform whose repeating nodules, potholes and horizontal beds become especially legible at low tide.
entities.description: The platform is geologically notable because the 1872 Hamada earthquake raised it roughly 1–1.5 m, exposing a geometric shore surface with calcareous nodules and potholes. Unlike a small outcrop, the feature occupies enough of the coast to read as a landscape. A coastal tunnel adds to the arrival experience.
entities.whyWorthwhile: Major-detour worthwhile for geology and unusual coastlines if timed for low tide and moderate seas. High water hides much of the pattern, so tide planning is part of the recommendation rather than a minor optimisation.

entities.summary: A seventh-century mountain fortress overlooking Asō Bay pairs with Tsushima's sacred quartz-porphyry summit for an unusually strong history-and-landscape combination.
entities.description: Kaneda Castle is a fortified mountain rather than a conventional keep: roughly 2.2 km of ancient walls and later military roads occupy ridges above a ria coast. Nearby Shiratake is a twin-peaked sacred mountain whose short approach becomes steep, rough and exposed near the summit. The two should be treated as complementary experiences, preferably on separate dry-weather outings rather than compressed into one rushed day.
entities.whyWorthwhile: Together they explain how Tsushima's border-island terrain shaped defence, religion and settlement. Kaneda provides archaeological depth and bay views; Shiratake adds the sharper physical and scenic climax.

entities.summary: Old ascetic paths link cave temples, cliff Buddhas, volcanic rock, farm basins and village roads into a sacred cultural landscape that works best as selected sections.
entities.description: The modern trail network extends roughly 135 km across ten sections, following terrain associated with the Rokugō Manzan ascetic tradition. Strong sections repeatedly combine rock sanctuaries, carved Buddhas, temples, ridges and old agricultural landscapes. The research does not recommend completionism: road walking, sparse resupply and uneven section quality make one to three carefully chosen stages a better visitor experience.
entities.whyWorthwhile: Few routes integrate geology, active religious heritage and lived rural landscape as densely. T1 is the clearest introduction; more rugged sections around T4/K1 add stronger ascetic atmosphere.

entities.summary: Long open sasa ridges, isolated ponds and broad undeveloped horizons make the quieter western Tsurugi range a superb clear-weather day for a strong hiker.
entities.description: After the forest climb toward Miune, the western ridge becomes unusually open: rounded bamboo-grass slopes continue through Tenguzuka to the broad Ushi-no-Se upland with little visible development. Practical versions run roughly 16–21 km and commonly require a shuttle or two vehicles. The route's value is highly weather-dependent because fog removes the continuous-ridge panorama that makes it exceptional.
entities.whyWorthwhile: Experienced Japanese hikers repeatedly singled out the western extension for solitude and sustained ridge quality rather than one summit. On a stable clear day it is a destination-worthy mountain journey.

entities.summary: A small Hokkaido wetland that can become extraordinary when tens of thousands of greater white-fronted geese leave or return to the communal roost around dawn and dusk.
entities.description: This is explicitly a temporal destination. The wetland is important outside migration, but the travel-worthy experience is the mass movement, sound and changing formations of the geese. Large numbers are reasonably reliable during the migration window; one perfectly synchronized departure is less reliable and can fragment under fog, rain or changing bird behaviour.
entities.whyWorthwhile: Major-detour worthwhile during the migration peak, usually mid-to-late April and late September to early October. Outside migration it should not consume scarce national travel time. Observe only from designated areas and follow local wildlife guidance.

entities.summary: One of Japan’s reliable “snow monster” landscapes, where heavily rimed trees form sculptural winter fields reached via the Ani gondola.
entities.description: The phenomenon requires sustained cold, wind-driven supercooled cloud and operating lift access. Formation is normal enough in season to plan around, but the actual experience still depends on visibility, wind and gondola operation; whiteout conditions can turn a spectacular landscape into almost nothing.
entities.whyWorthwhile: Major-detour worthwhile in a good winter weather window, roughly early January to early March. Treat forecast and lift operation as first-class constraints and keep schedule flexibility rather than assuming the phenomenon guarantees visibility on a fixed day.

entities.summary: A rural landscape where former iron-sand extraction terrain was deliberately reworked into rice terraces, channels and productive fields.
entities.description: This is an unusually good example of industrial history becoming difficult to see precisely because landscape rehabilitation succeeded. Without interpretation it can look like merely attractive countryside; with a museum, guide or prior reading, residual hill forms, channels and terraced fields become evidence of the old kanna-nagashi iron-sand process.
entities.whyWorthwhile: Major-detour worthwhile for landscape/history interests, ideally as a half- or full-day car journey linking a tatara museum or furnace site with the agricultural terrain. Green rice season, harvest gold and autumn all work. The experience is weaker if treated as one viewpoint without context.

entities.summary: A genuinely destination-scale indoor aquatic resort combining big pools and slides, child water zones, hot-water bathing and permanent Polynesian stage entertainment.
entities.description: This is much more than a hotel pool: a 50 m main pool, multiple body and tube slides, family water areas and other paid water activities support a full day, while live Polynesian shows give the complex a distinctive identity. Much of the core experience is weather-independent.
entities.whyWorthwhile: A major regional destination and one of Japan’s most substantial all-weather aquatic attractions. Summer and holiday crowds, swim logistics and extra-charge activities can materially affect value, but the breadth justifies a dedicated visit for water-loving families and adults.

entities.summary: A real mountain approach opens abruptly into a broad high moor of pools, winding channels and boardwalk, making the wetland feel far larger than a roadside marsh.
entities.description: The route climbs from Uryūnuma Gate Park before entering the high wetland and looping the boardwalk among ponds and the meandering Penkepetan River. The bundled line geometry is the current wetland circuit only. It intentionally does not continue over the South Shokanbetsu–Shokanbetsu segment, which was closed for the 2026 season.
entities.whyWorthwhile: The transition from enclosed forest climb to a wide, elevated moor is the experience. Flower season and September autumn grass both give the pools and mountain enclosure enough scale to justify a dedicated detour.

entities.summary: A vast reconstructed Yayoi-period moated settlement where archaeology is made tangible through buildings, landscape and hands-on ancient-life activities.
entities.description: The scale of the reconstructed settlement is the main differentiator: visitors move through gates, watchtowers and residential or ritual zones rather than seeing isolated artefacts in cases. Making magatama, fire-making and other activities add practical texture, while large play lawns make the site unusually workable for families.
entities.whyWorthwhile: A major regional destination and one of Japan’s strongest experiential archaeological sites. The large outdoor footprint is a virtue in mild weather but becomes a real heat, rain and walking consideration in summer.

entities.description: Eleven themed buildings gather regional crafts and making activities inside relocated Edo- and Meiji-period houses. Visitors can choose from many short workshops rather than committing to a single specialist class, which makes traditional production unusually approachable for mixed-age groups.
entities.whyWorthwhile: A major regional destination for hands-on culture and one of the strongest multi-craft complexes in Japan. Workshop charges accumulate and not every activity suits every age, but the density and variety make the detour worthwhile.

entities.description: Daytime house-company performances and rotating evening appearances by established dance groups make the dance itself the centrepiece, while the museum provides context. Regular shows include a participation segment, so the visit is more active than a conventional performing-arts display.
entities.whyWorthwhile: An excellent compact cultural experience for visitors who will not be in Tokushima during the main August festival. entities.summary: A clear-water river journey linking a giant monolith, dense pothole fields, low submersible bridges and forested valley scenery.
entities.description: Individual search results fragment Kozagawa into short roadside geosites. The stronger unit is the half- or full-day river corridor: Ichimai-iwa gives immediate monumental scale, Takinohai provides a patterned bedrock field and the route between them keeps the clear river and valley present. Kayaking can add another perspective when water and operators align.
entities.whyWorthwhile: Strong regional discovery because the pieces reinforce each other, but not worth a cross-country journey for one roadside stop alone. Visit in dry stable weather when the river is clear; post-rain turbidity weakens much of the visual appeal.

entities.summary: A museum-and-performance pairing that turns Oga’s Namahage tradition into a vivid encounter with masks, ritual context and a live household demonstration.
entities.description: The museum explains regional mask forms and the living tradition; next door, the Shinzan folklore museum stages the New Year household visit inside a traditional magariya house. The physical performance communicates strongly even when spoken Japanese is only partly understood.
entities.whyWorthwhile: One of the strongest permanent ways to experience a living regional folk tradition outside festival dates. The demonstration can be loud and intimidating for sensitive young children, and the folklore museum has limited capacity.

entities.summary: A long granite gorge of white slabs, clear pools, channels and broad sliding waterfalls in southwest Shikoku.
entities.description: Validation downgraded the famous Yukiwa Falls as a standalone target: specialist waterfall evidence reports that it can lack power in low water. The broader gorge survives that criticism because the granite river environment continues for kilometres and can be experienced as a walk or, with a legitimate operator and suitable conditions, canyoning.
entities.whyWorthwhile: Strong regional discovery when approached as a gorge landscape rather than a single waterfall. Dry-to-normal water, warm-season greenery and enough time to walk beyond one viewpoint produce the best reward.

entities.summary: An intimate Chōkai foothill ecosystem of giant pollarded beeches, abundant cold springs and a globally unusual moss community.
entities.description: The immediate visual payoff comes from the huge multi-stemmed beeches and spring-fed forest. The rare “Chōkai marimo” moss community is scientifically remarkable but visually subtler and benefits strongly from interpretation. The boardwalk/forest circuit is roughly 5 km and 2–3 hours.
entities.whyWorthwhile: A strong regional discovery rather than a national must-see for everyone. It becomes much more compelling for botany, forest ecology or vernacular woodland-use interests. Stay on boardwalks and marked routes; confirm any damaged or restricted sections before visiting.
